# Daggerfall decompilation

<!-- progress:start -->
![decompiled](https://img.shields.io/badge/decompiled-100.00%25-brightgreen) ![functions](https://img.shields.io/badge/functions-2297%20of%202297-brightgreen) ![FALL.EXE](https://img.shields.io/badge/FALL.EXE-matching-brightgreen)

100.00% of the game's own code (580076 of 580076 bytes, 2297 of 2297 functions) is matched C; the rebuilt `FALL.EXE` is byte-identical to 1.07.213.
<!-- progress:end -->

A matching decompilation of *The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall* (DOS, 1996), starting with the game
executable `FALL.EXE` (version 1.07.213), built with Watcom C32 10.0a and run under the CauseWay
DOS extender. The rebuild uses that same compiler, run under DOSBox-X.

This repo contains no game files (executables or data) and no compiler. You supply the
executables and your own copies of Watcom C/C++ 10.0a and, for the XnGine engine, Borland Turbo
Assembler 4.0; the tools check the executables' SHA-1.

- [docs/head_start.md](docs/head_start.md): the research plan this project started from
- [docs/progress.md](docs/progress.md): a log of what has been found and done, newest last
- [docs/xngine.md](docs/xngine.md): the XnGine engine (object 2): plan and log
- [docs/xngine_readable.md](docs/xngine_readable.md): XnGine as readable C: how it runs, is declared and tested; [docs/engine/](docs/engine/): its data structures and the designs for its self-modifying code
- [docs/play.md](docs/play.md): playing the headless game with tools/fallplay.py: commands, start points, UI facts
- [docs/state.md](docs/state.md): where the game keeps its state in memory (player, character record, mode, location), with the evidence for each
- [docs/naming.md](docs/naming.md): the naming convention for functions, globals and record fields
- [docs/port.md](docs/port.md): the native port (arm64 macOS, SDL3): how it builds, its rules and status
- [docs/natural_c.md](docs/natural_c.md): making the lifted C read like real C (structuring, typed globals, local names, declarations) and the Watcom 10.0a control-flow rules

## Status

- `FALL.EXE` 1.07.213 reproduced from Bethesda's free release (`c49a2ceb…`).
- Format: uncompressed LE behind the CauseWay stub. 3 objects, 37,520 fixups.
- 3,315 functions found in object 1 (98.4% of its bytes decoded): 2,297 of them are the
  game's own C in 84 original source units (names recovered from `__FILE__` strings), the
  rest are libraries (MemCheck, Watcom runtime). Object 2 is the XnGine engine, hand-written
  asm assembled with Borland TASM 4.0: all of it is rebuilt from `src/xngine/` (113 modules,
  719 functions, every address a symbol, the self-modifying code's patch fields named).
- Compiler: Watcom C32 10.0a. Game code is unoptimised, with debug info: `-od -s -of+ -4r -d2`.
- Toolchain: the real Watcom C32 10.0a `wcc386` (and `wasm` for the two assembly helpers)
  under DOSBox-X (`tools/wcc10.py`): one DOSBox-X run compiles all of `src/` in under a minute.
- Sources: `src/lifted/` holds the functions `tools/lift.py` lifted and the compiler
  matched, one file per unit. It was generated until 2026-10-04 and is now ordinary source,
  with names and record structs edited in (`promote_lifted.py` refuses to overwrite it).
  `src/hand/` holds functions matched by hand, one per file; `src/<unit>.c` are
  hand-written units; `src/int.asm` is the original's assembly; `src/xngine/` is object 2,
  generated by `tools/xn_disasm.py`; `src/xngine_c/` is object 2 as literal C, generated by
  `tools/xn_c.py` and checked against 8,204 recorded calls (not part of FALL.EXE's build).
  `src/engine/` is object 2 as readable C (`tools/xn_rc.py`, docs/xngine_readable.md): every
  function written as C a person would write, checked against the same records and in lockstep
  frames of the game.
- Matched game functions and the share of game code: see the badges at the top (updated by
  every successful `tools/build-and-verify.sh`); the rebuilt executable is byte-identical.

## Quick start

```sh
# 1. Game files: Bethesda's DFInstall.zip in orig/, then run the 1.07.213 patcher
#    headless in DOSBox-X (brew install dosbox-x)
tools/patch_213.sh orig/DFInstall.zip

# 2. Python tools
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. The compiler: from your Watcom C/C++ 10.0a media, copy WATCOM/BIN, WATCOM/BINB and
#    WATCOM/H to third_party/watcom10/w10a/WATCOM/ (never committed)
#    The assembler for object 2: from your TASM 4.0 disks, unpack CMD16.PAK and CMDLINE.PAK
#    (LHA archives; tar -xf reads them) into third_party/tasm/BIN/ (never committed).
#    Without it the build keeps object 2's original bytes.
#    For the headless game (tools/fallemu.py): a patched Unicorn, about a minute to build,
#    which runs the 3D world ~70x faster than the pip one (needs cmake and ninja)
tools/build_unicorn.sh

# 4. Find functions and units, match a C file, then build and verify
.venv/bin/python tools/find_functions.py
.venv/bin/python tools/find_units.py
.venv/bin/python tools/split.py                # asm listings in asm/nonmatchings/
.venv/bin/python tools/lift_all.py               # batch: lift, compile, check
.venv/bin/python tools/settle_lifted.py          # matched → src/lifted/ (how it was built; now frozen)
tools/build-and-verify.sh
```

## Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `tools/patch_213.sh` | build the 1.07.213 `FALL.EXE` from `DFInstall.zip` |
| `tools/wcc10.py` | run Watcom C32 10.0a (and WASM) under DOSBox-X; check files against `FALL.EXE` |
| `tools/w10_try.py` | try many C variants of one function in one compiler run |
| `tools/w10_frame.py` | predict 10.0a's stack-frame layout from a function's declarations |
| `tools/le.py` | LE loader: objects, pages, fixups (from KKND-Decomp) |
| `tools/find_functions.py` | function discovery → `config/functions.csv` |
| `tools/split.py` | one symbolic asm listing per function → `asm/nonmatchings/` (gitignored) |
| `tools/omf.py` | OMF object reader (from KKND-Decomp) |
| `tools/match.py` | compile a C file and compare its functions with `FALL.EXE` |
| `tools/cc_dis.py` | disassemble what the compiler makes of a C file |
| `tools/find_units.py`, `tools/units.py` | recover the original source units; map an address to its unit |
| `tools/lift.py`, `tools/lift_all.py` | lift `-od` code to C; batch lift, compile and check every game function (2 s) |
| `tools/promote_lifted.py`, `tools/settle_lifted.py` | write matched lifted functions into `src/lifted/<unit>.c`, splitting out any that match only on their own |
| `tools/update_readme_progress.py` | refresh the README badges from `build/progress.json` |
| `tools/build-and-verify.sh` | splice all of `src/` into `FALL.EXE` and check the SHA-1 (`build_fall.py`) |
| `tools/xn_disasm.py` | disassemble object 2 (XnGine) into TASM modules in `src/xngine/` that reassemble to the original |
| `tools/xn_link.py` | assemble the XnGine modules with TASM 4.0 under DOSBox-X and check bytes and fixups |
| `tools/fallemu.py` | run `FALL.EXE` headless (Unicorn): DOS, DPMI, timer, keyboard and mouse, scripted scenarios |
| `tools/fallplay.py` | play the headless game a step at a time (snapshots, rewind, 2x screenshots, new code per step), for a model at the controls (walk, turn, go to and enter buildings); `FALLEMU_CHEAT=1` boots with the game's cheat mode |
| `tools/fallcov.py` | code coverage of the headless game: which functions ran, per source unit and XnGine module |
| `tools/fallfuzz.py` | coverage-guided random play: workers play random input from the save snapshots and keep every state that ran new code |
| `tools/fallevidence.py` | evidence for naming: replays every play step and fuzz state with coverage, then gives each function the inputs that go with it running, its cluster, callers, callees and strings, and the asset evidence: files read, texts and sounds asked for, button boxes handled |
| `tools/fallcall.py` | call any function in a live game from a safe point between frames: return value, functions run, files opened, globals changed, the screen it draws; `sweep` does it for many functions, each from a fresh game |
| `tools/fallassets.py` | asset tracing: replays every evidence episode and loads every classic save with each file read (and each sound asked for) attributed to its validated guest call chain and named by record; `report` lists per asset class the loaders and consumers, per function the assets it reads |
| `tools/asset_ids.py` | static asset evidence, no emulator: the TEXT.RSC records and sounds each function asks for by constant id (with the text or sound name), the screen button tables `{x0,y0,x1,y1,handler}` and the text-macro tables |
| `tools/assets.py` | readers for the game's data files: BSA and DAGGER.SND records, TEXT.RSC text, TEXTURE archives, sound names (`config/sound_clips.csv`, from Daggerfall Unity) |
| `tools/libmatch.py` | names the library region's Watcom runtime functions by matching them, relocations masked, against Watcom C32 10.0a's own libraries (extracted from the 10.0a CD into third_party/) |
| `tools/structure.py` | rewrites the lifter's gotos as if/else, &&/||, while, do-while, for, break and continue, keeping each function byte-identical (it compiles every change with Watcom 10.0a) |
| `tools/type_globals.py` | types `extern char g[];` globals as scalars, arrays or mixed types and removes their casts, verified per file |
| `tools/protos.py` | makes each file's declarations of a function agree with its definition, keeping what still compiles to FALL.EXE's bytes; `unify` searches for one prototype every file matches with |
| `tools/apply_names.py` | puts the confirmed and strong names from config/names.csv into src/ and include/, recording them in config/symbols.txt for the build (re-runnable; `revert` puts addresses back) |
| `tools/names.py` | config/names.csv: names for functions, globals and record fields, each with a confidence and its evidence (check, merge, show, annotate) |
| `tools/fallstate.py` | experiments that find game state in memory: screens, interaction modes, values read off the screen, counters that move in step |
| `tools/memwatch.py` | memory watchdog: kills this repo's emulator processes, largest first, before the machine runs out of memory (the multi-worker tools start it themselves) |
| `tools/build_unicorn.sh` | build the patched Unicorn `fallemu.py` uses (`tools/unicorn/dagger-unicorn.patch`): ~70x faster in the 3D world |
| `tools/xn_trace.py`, `tools/xn_record.py` | XnGine code coverage and run-time code writes; record and replay single calls |
| `tools/xn_abi.py` | XnGine's register interfaces (`config/xngine_abi.csv`): inputs, outputs, flags and clobbers per function, from liveness over both objects, checked on the record corpus by scrambling |
| `tools/xn_rc.py` | XnGine as readable C (`src/engine/`): build with Watcom 10.0a, route the asm's calls to the C, test against the records by each function's interface, differential tests, lockstep frames against the asm (`frames`) |
| `tools/xn_declcheck.py` | the `#pragma aux` interfaces the readable C's files give a function, against its definition's |
| `tools/xn_c.py`, `tools/xn_cload.py` | XnGine as C: translate every function to literal C (`src/xngine_c/`), compile it with Watcom 10.0a, and replay the record corpus, differential tests or the game itself with XnGine in C |
| `tools/port_build.py` | the native build (docs/port.md): the game's C with clang and SDL3, stubs and data generated for what the port lacks; `run` starts it on a game folder |
| `tools/port_census.py` | the native build's 64-bit worklist: clang's diagnostics on the game's C, by kind and file |

Several tools are adapted from [KKND-Decomp](https://github.com/Wyrelade/KKND-Decomp) (CC0).

# NETWARS – modernized build notes

This repository contains the original reverse-engineered DOS-era NetWars assets, plus a modernized Linux build path designed for contemporary desktops, 4K displays, and Debian Linux Trixie.

## What changed

- Added a modern SDL2 launcher for contemporary operating systems.
- Added a 4K-capable render loop with a starfield background and HUD shell.
- Added CMake build support for Debian Linux Trixie and other modern Unix-like systems.
- Kept the original DOS reverse-engineering files intact for historical reference.

## Supported environments

- Debian Linux Trixie
- Ubuntu 24.04+ / Debian 12+
- macOS 13+
- Windows 10/11 with SDL2 available

## Prerequisites

On Debian Trixie:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake pkg-config libsdl2-dev
```

## Build

```bash
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build
```

## Run

```bash
./build/netwars-modern
```

The launcher opens a modern window with a 4K logical canvas (3840x2160) and scales cleanly on high-DPI screens.

## Notes

This modern build is intentionally a playable baseline and modernization layer rather than a direct port of the original Borland C++ DOS code. The DOS-era files remain in `NETWARS/` and are preserved as reverse-engineering artifacts.

The original Reverse-Engineered Source Code project is still available in the `NETWARS/` directory and is not replaced by this modern runtime.

Outstanding implementation work is tracked in [tasks.md](tasks.md).

# RYSSÄN KAUHU – portable C / SDL2 port

A reverse-engineered, portable re-implementation of **RYSSÄN KAUHU**, a Finnish
DOS shooter from the 1990s. The game is set in the Winter War: you sit behind
a machine gun and stop the waves of Soviet soldiers walking towards you across an
open field. Graphics by Tuomas Aikioniemi, sound by Aleksi Ala-Mononen
("this product has been finded by sheepart's products").

The port is a function-by-function translation of the original 32-bit Watcom C
program (disassembled from `RYSS.EXE`, a DOS/4GW LE executable) to C99, with SDL2
standing in for VGA mode 13h, the 100 Hz timer interrupt, the keyboard interrupt,
the INT 33h mouse driver and the Sound Blaster. The hand-written asm module of the
original (sprite scaler, font, Sound Blaster mixer) is re-implemented in
`src/gfx.c` and `src/sound.c`. See `docs/REVERSE_ENGINEERING.md` for the details.

**You need the original game files.** The port reads `GRAPH.DAT` at runtime
(graphics, fonts, sounds and lookup tables are all in it).

## Play in the browser

**[Play RYSSÄN KAUHU in your browser](https://klassikkopelit.github.io/RyssanKauhu/)**,
no installation or game files needed. Works on phones and tablets too: touch
the screen to aim and fire, tap to continue when the game waits for a key
(start, next level, new game), and use the Esc button to quit. Turn the device
sideways for a bigger picture.

## Download

Version 1.0.0:

- [Windows (64-bit)](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/RyssanKauhu/releases/download/v1.0.0/ryssankauhu-v1.0.0-windows-x64.zip)
- [macOS (Apple silicon and Intel)](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/RyssanKauhu/releases/download/v1.0.0/ryssankauhu-v1.0.0-macos-universal.zip)
- [Linux (64-bit)](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/RyssanKauhu/releases/download/v1.0.0/ryssankauhu-v1.0.0-linux-x64.zip)

All versions: [Releases](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/RyssanKauhu/releases).
You also need the original `GRAPH.DAT`, see `readme.txt` in the zip.

## Building

Requirements: a C99 compiler, CMake ≥ 3.10 and SDL2 (2.0.10 or newer).

### Linux
```sh
sudo apt install build-essential cmake libsdl2-dev     # Debian/Ubuntu
# sudo dnf install gcc cmake SDL2-devel                # Fedora
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
```

### macOS
```sh
brew install cmake sdl2
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
```

### Windows – Visual Studio
Install SDL2 with vcpkg (`vcpkg install sdl2:x64-windows`) or download
`SDL2-devel-2.x.x-VC.zip` from <https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/releases>, then
```bat
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=C:/vcpkg/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake
rem   or: -DSDL2_DIR=C:/SDL2-2.x.x/cmake
cmake --build build --config Release
```
`SDL2.dll` is copied next to `ryssankauhu-sdl.exe` automatically.

### Windows – MinGW / MSYS2
```sh
pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-SDL2
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles" && cmake --build build
```

There is also a plain makefile for systems with `sdl2-config`: `make -f Makefile.unix`.

### Web version (WebAssembly)

Install [Emscripten](https://emscripten.org/docs/getting_started/downloads.html)
(version 6.0.12 is what the GitHub workflow uses), then:
```sh
source ~/emsdk/emsdk_env.sh            # once per terminal window
emcmake cmake -S . -B build-web -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build-web
python3 -m http.server -d build-web 8000
```
and open <http://localhost:8000>. The page has to come from a web server;
opening `index.html` straight from disk does not work. `assets/GRAPH.DAT` is
packed into the page (`index.data`). On touch screens a finger aims and fires,
and while the game waits for a key (Enter, Space, K) a tap presses it
(`plat_waiting_for_key()` in `src/platform.c`); the page adds an Esc button.
The web-only code is inside `#ifdef __EMSCRIPTEN__` blocks and in
`web/shell.html`, so the desktop builds are unchanged.

### Prebuilt releases (GitHub Actions)

`.github/workflows/build-release.yml` builds Windows (x64), macOS (universal)
and Linux (x64) zips on every push to `main` and on pull requests; the zips are
attached to the workflow run as artifacts. Pushing a version tag also publishes
them as a GitHub release:
```sh
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
```
Each zip holds the executable, `readme.txt` (from `packaging/`), the
libraries it needs (`SDL2.dll` on Windows; on macOS and Linux SDL2 is linked
statically) and an empty `data/` folder for the original game file, which is
never included.

`.github/workflows/web.yml` builds the web version and publishes it on GitHub
Pages on every push to `main` (one-time setup: Settings → Pages → Source:
"GitHub Actions").

## Running

The program is called `ryssankauhu-sdl`. Run it inside the folder with
`GRAPH.DAT`, or give the folder as an argument:
```sh
./build/ryssankauhu-sdl /path/to/ryssankauhu
./build/ryssankauhu-sdl --fullscreen --sens 1.5 /path/to/ryssankauhu
```
If no argument is given the game looks in the current directory, then next to
the executable, then in a `data` folder next to the executable. So you can
either put `GRAPH.DAT` into a `data` folder beside `ryssankauhu-sdl.exe` (the
layout of the release zips), or drop the program into the original game folder,
and double-click it.

Controls are those of the original:

| | |
|---|---|
| Mouse | aim |
| Left button or Ctrl | fire |
| Left / Right arrow | aim with the keyboard |
| Enter | start (title screen) |
| Space | next level |
| K / E | new game? yes (*kyllä*) / no (*ei*) |
| Esc | quit |
| Alt+Enter, F11 | toggle fullscreen |

Eight hits and you are dead (the red crosses at the bottom left). Once per level
a medic patches you up, and an empty gun gets 50 more rounds five seconds later.
Clear six levels to win. *KUOLIT* = you died, *KENTTÄ LÄPI!* = level cleared,
*Paina välilyöntiä* = press space, *VOITIT!!!* = you won, *Uusi peli (k/e)?* =
new game (y/n)?

## How faithful is it?

* Same screens, texts (in Finnish), colours, layout and timings: the game logic
  runs on the original's 100 Hz timer, with the original level table, spawn
  logic, enemy accuracy table and hit detection.
* The renderer keeps the original's four-buffer, dirty-row scheme, and the
  scaled sprite routine reproduces the original's 8.8 fixed point stepping, so
  the soldiers look pixel for pixel the same.
* Sound goes through a C copy of the original two-voice Sound Blaster mixer
  (8000 Hz, 8-bit), including the machine gun loop and the rule that only the
  important sounds may interrupt one already playing.
* The "SIVARI" cheat still works.

Small, deliberate differences:
* Sprites are clipped at the screen edges (the original let them wrap around).
* The mouse is read in relative mode and scaled so that sweeping it across the
  window covers the whole field of fire, like the original's doubled mouse
  speed did on a 640-wide mouse range. `--sens` adjusts it.
* The Gravis Ultrasound code is not ported; sound always uses the SB path.
* The "Loading: ......" text the original printed while reading `GRAPH.DAT` in
  text mode is not shown.

## Source layout

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `src/game.c` | game logic, translated function by function (original addresses in comments) |
| `src/gfx.c` | the asm module's sprite, scaled sprite, font and screen copy routines |
| `src/sound.c` | Sound Blaster sample setup and the two-voice mixer |
| `src/data.c` | `GRAPH.DAT` loader and decryption |
| `src/platform.c` | SDL2: VGA mode 13h, PIT timer, keyboard interrupt, INT 33h mouse, audio |
| `src/files.c` | case-insensitive access to the DOS file names |
| `tools/le_unpack.py` | loads `RYSS.EXE`, applies the LE fixups and writes a flat image for disassembly |
| `tools/extract_assets.py` | dumps sprites, background, fonts and sounds from `GRAPH.DAT` to PNG/WAV |
| `web/shell.html` | the web page around the WebAssembly version |
| `assets/` | the original game files: `GRAPH.DAT` (packed into the web version) and `RYSS.EXE` |

# INVATAXI – portable C / SDL2 port

A reverse-engineered, portable re-implementation of **INVATAXI** (Åkesoft, 1994),
a Finnish DOS mouse game where you drive an "invataxi" and have to understand
where your mumbling passenger wants to go.

The port is a function-by-function translation of the original Turbo Pascal 6
program (disassembled from `INVATAXI.EXE`) to C99, with SDL2 standing in for
VGA, the Crt unit, the INT 33h mouse driver and the Sound Blaster. The MOD
player "PaxiMod" that was linked into the game is re-implemented in
`src/modplayer.c`. See `docs/REVERSE_ENGINEERING.md` for the details.

**You need the original game files.** The port reads them at runtime:
`INVATAXI.EXE`, `HJUVA_#1.EXE`, `HJUVA_#2.EXE`, `HARMONIA.NVA`,
`HISCORE.NVA` and `1.SKP` … `24.SKP`. The pictures are unpacked straight out of
the PKLITE-compressed EXEs, so nothing has to be extracted by hand.

## Play in the browser

**[Play INVATAXI in your browser](https://klassikkopelit.github.io/invataxi/)**,
no installation or game files needed. Works on phones and tablets too: tap a
menu line to choose it, tap the map to pick the destination, tap anywhere else
to continue or stop the taxi, and use the Esc button to give up. The name for
the high-score list is typed into a field that opens the on-screen keyboard.

## Download

Version 1.0.0:

- [Windows (64-bit)](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/invataxi/releases/download/v1.0.0/invataxi-v1.0.0-windows-x64.zip)
- [macOS (Apple silicon and Intel)](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/invataxi/releases/download/v1.0.0/invataxi-v1.0.0-macos-universal.zip)
- [Linux (64-bit)](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/invataxi/releases/download/v1.0.0/invataxi-v1.0.0-linux-x64.zip)

All versions: [Releases](https://github.com/klassikkopelit/invataxi/releases).
You also need the original INVATAXI game files, see `readme.txt` in the zip.

## Original game files

You can download the original game files from [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/invataxi)

## Building

Requirements: a C99 compiler, CMake ≥ 3.10 and SDL2 (2.0.10 or newer).

### Linux
```sh
sudo apt install build-essential cmake libsdl2-dev     # Debian/Ubuntu
# sudo dnf install gcc cmake SDL2-devel                # Fedora
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
```

### macOS
```sh
brew install cmake sdl2
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
```

### Windows – Visual Studio
Install SDL2 with vcpkg (`vcpkg install sdl2:x64-windows`) or download
`SDL2-devel-2.x.x-VC.zip` from <https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/releases>, then
```bat
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=C:/vcpkg/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake
rem   or: -DSDL2_DIR=C:/SDL2-2.x.x/cmake
cmake --build build --config Release
```
`SDL2.dll` is copied next to `invataxi-sdl.exe` automatically.

### Windows – MinGW / MSYS2
```sh
pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-SDL2
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles" && cmake --build build
```

There is also a plain makefile for systems with `sdl2-config`: `make -f Makefile.unix`.

### Web version (WebAssembly)

Install [Emscripten](https://emscripten.org/docs/getting_started/downloads.html)
(version 6.0.12 is what the GitHub workflow uses), then:
```sh
source ~/emsdk/emsdk_env.sh            # once per terminal window
emcmake cmake -S . -B build-web -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build-web
python3 -m http.server -d build-web 8000
```
and open <http://localhost:8000>. The page has to come from a web server;
opening `index.html` straight from disk does not work. The original game
files in `assets/` are packed into the page (`index.data`), and high scores
are kept in the browser's local storage. On touch screens a tap becomes a
key press except on the map (`touch_tap_as_key()` in `src/platform.c`), and
the page adds an Esc button and a name field. The web-only code is inside
`#ifdef __EMSCRIPTEN__` blocks and in `web/shell.html`, so the desktop builds
are unchanged.

### Prebuilt releases (GitHub Actions)

`.github/workflows/build-release.yml` builds Windows (x64), macOS (universal)
and Linux (x64) zips on every push to `main` and on pull requests; the zips are
attached to the workflow run as artifacts. Pushing a version tag also publishes
them as a GitHub release:
```sh
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
```
Each zip holds the executable, `readme.txt` (from `packaging/`), the
libraries it needs (`SDL2.dll` on Windows; on macOS and Linux SDL2 is linked
statically) and an empty `data/` folder for the original game files, which are
never included.

`.github/workflows/web.yml` builds the web version and publishes it on GitHub
Pages on every push to `main` (one-time setup: Settings → Pages → Source:
"GitHub Actions").

## Running

The program is called `invataxi-sdl` so that it can never overwrite the
original `INVATAXI.EXE` (on Windows file names ignore case), which it needs.

Run `invataxi-sdl` inside the folder with the original files, or give the folder
as an argument:
```sh
./build/invataxi-sdl /path/to/invataxi
./build/invataxi-sdl --sound-menu /path/to/invataxi   # with the original sound menu
```
If no argument is given the game looks in the current directory, then next to
the executable, then in a `data` folder next to the executable. So you can
either put the original files into a `data` folder beside `invataxi-sdl.exe`
and `SDL2.dll` (the layout of the release zips), or drop those two files into
the original game folder, and double-click the exe. `HISCORE.NVA` is updated in
place, as in the original.

Controls are those of the original: number keys in the menus, the left mouse
button on the map, any key to stop the taxi, ESC to give up.
`Alt+Enter` or `F11` toggles fullscreen.

## How faithful is it?

* Same screens, texts (in Finnish), colours, layout and timings (everything is
  counted in 70 Hz vertical retraces, like the original).
* The two helper programs `HJUVA_#1.EXE` / `HJUVA_#2.EXE` that the game
  `Exec`s to put a picture on screen are emulated by drawing the same
  picture.
* The original sound card / mixing rate menu is skipped: the game starts
  straight away as if you had picked Sound Blaster at 22000 Hz. Run
  `invataxi-sdl --sound-menu` to get the original menu back (the chosen rate is
  then used, and "4. Ilman ääniä" plays without sound, as in the original).
* All of the original's quirks are kept on purpose: the score is a random
  number, getting on the high-score list is a coin toss, the list position is
  random, and ESC plus a wrong answer can push lives below zero.

Small, deliberate differences:
* Text mode uses the IBM VGA 8×16 font (from VileR's
  [VGA text mode fonts](https://github.com/viler-int10h/vga-text-mode-fonts)).
* The mouse pointer is drawn black/white regardless of the palette.
* Very short clicks that start and end between two frames are not lost.
* If `HISCORE.NVA` is missing, the default table is shown instead of the
  original's "Runtime error 002".
* The farewell text stays on screen for 1.5 s before the window closes.
* Keys pressed before the high-score name prompt appears are ignored, so they
  don't end up at the start of the name (the original kept them).

## Source layout

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `src/game.c` | game logic, translated procedure by procedure (original offsets in comments) |
| `src/modplayer.c` | PaxiMod-compatible ProTracker player + speech/effect channel |
| `src/platform.c` | SDL2: VGA mode 13h / text mode, Crt, keyboard, mouse, timing, audio |
| `src/pklite.c` | PKLITE 1.12 unpacker used to read the pictures from the EXEs |
| `src/files.c` | case-insensitive access to the DOS file names |
| `src/font_vga.h`, `src/cp437.h`, `src/periods.h` | font, code page and period tables |
| `web/shell.html` | the web page around the WebAssembly version |
| `assets/` | the original game files, packed into the web version |

# Welltris (1989) — decompilation & multiplatform port

Welltris is Alexey Pajitnov's three-dimensional follow-up to Tetris: pieces slide down the four
walls of a well and onto its 8×8 floor, where full rows *and* columns clear. Walls that a piece
sticks to freeze for three turns; four frozen walls end the game. This repo is a
reverse-engineered port of the DOS version (Spectrum HoloByte, 1989) to portable C + SDL2: it
runs natively on Linux, Windows and macOS, and in a browser via WebAssembly. No original game
files are included or needed to play.

**Play in the browser:** <https://rembish.github.io/welltris-revamp/> (phones and tablets get
on-screen controls).

![A search bot playing the homage version until all four walls freeze](docs/demo.gif)

*The test bot (`tests/botgen.c`) playing at speed 1 with the homage pictures: 30 lines and two
level-ups, until all four walls freeze. [Full-quality video](docs/demo.mp4).*

The goal has two halves:

1. **Game logic: decompiled faithfully.** Piece sets, the Turbo C random number generator and
   how it is used, spawning, moves and rotation (quirks included), gravity and drops on the
   original's 187 Hz timer, wall freezing and thawing, pieces sliding down thawed walls, floor
   line clears, scoring, level ups and the timing of every blocking effect. This is a
   deterministic, platform-independent C core that is checked pass by pass against the
   original machine code (see [How faithful is it?](#how-faithful-is-it)).
2. **Presentation: modernized.** The well and the panel are drawn fresh at any resolution. The
   pictures are a homage: the original's Moscow became Prague (the title over the Vltava, a
   hockey arena for the set-up screen, five Prague scenes for the five speeds, a pub for the hall
   of fame). The original artwork can be upscaled from *your own copy* into a private build.

## Layout

| Path        | Contents |
|-------------|----------|
| `core/`     | Game logic reconstructed from `WELLTRIS.EXE`: plain C99, no I/O, deterministic |
| `src/`      | SDL2 frontend: rendering, input, PC-speaker sound, menus, hall of fame, touch controls |
| `tests/`    | Replay tool and a search bot used by the differential test |
| `assets/`   | Font and the homage pictures (`assets/art`, see [`docs/art-brief.md`](docs/art-brief.md)) |
| `web/`      | HTML shell for the browser build |
| `re/`       | Reverse-engineering notes, Ghidra scripts, table generator, emulator harness, asset tool |

## The original

The tools in `re/` need your own copy of the DOS release in `original/` (git-ignored, never
distributed). The executable they were written against:

```
6a977c98cb17bd612cca4ffa293c65a1d9020236460a03bc313881f51f90bcd0  welltris.exe
```

- `welltris.exe` is the whole game: Turbo C 2.0, small model, one 50 KB executable.
- `*.bin` / `t-*.bin` are the pictures for EGA and for the 320×200 modes (RLE-packed planar
  images). All game rules live in the executable; none of them are in the pictures.
- The game asks a manual-lookup question at start ("the capital of this republic…") and checks
  the answer again on every piece and in the menu. The port leaves the protection out (it
  keeps the two random numbers it draws, so the piece sequence is unaffected).

## Playing

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| Arrow keys / keypad 8 2 4 6 / I M J L | move the piece along the wall it is on |
| K / keypad 5 | rotate |
| Space | drop |
| Alt+P or Esc | pause |
| Alt+N | next piece preview on/off (the preview costs 5 points per piece) |
| Alt+M | move mode: arrows follow the screen (1) or always left/right (2) |
| Alt+S | sound on/off |
| Alt+A / Alt+R | abort / restart the game |
| Alt+Q | quit |
| F11 / Alt+Enter | fullscreen |

As in the original, `5` turns the piece one quarter and `K` three quarters (the key code is
passed on as the number of turns). On a touch screen the same actions are on-screen buttons.

The set-up screen is the original's: LEVEL 1–3 picks the piece set (small pieces and
tetrominoes, tetrominoes, everything up to pentominoes), SPEED 1.0–5.0 the starting speed. Scores
and options are stored per user (`~/.local/share/Welltris/Welltris/` on Linux,
`%APPDATA%\Welltris\Welltris\` on Windows, browser storage on the web) in the original formats,
so `scores.bin` and `options.bin` from the DOS version can be copied there. Unlike the original,
which only wrote scores when you quit cleanly, the port saves them straight away.

## Building

Native (Linux, macOS, Windows with any SDL2 package):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j
./build/welltris
```

Browser (Emscripten):

```sh
source ~/tools/emsdk/emsdk_env.sh
emcmake cmake -S . -B build-web
cmake --build build-web -j --target welltris
cd build-web && python3 -m http.server   # open http://localhost:8000/welltris.html
```

### With the original artwork (private builds only)

```sh
python3 -m venv ~/tools/venv --system-site-packages
~/tools/venv/bin/pip install vtracer resvg-py opencv-python-headless numpy pillow
~/tools/venv/bin/python re/tools/assets.py build          # needs original/*.bin
cmake -S . -B build-local -DWT_LOCAL_ASSETS=ON && cmake --build build-local -j
```

`assets.py` decodes the pictures and upscales them 3× to 4:3 into the git-ignored
`assets-local/`: line art (frames, panels) is traced into vectors and re-rendered, dithered
pictures (title, scenes, set-up, hall of fame) are de-dithered and sharpened. Such a build uses
the original screens and layouts instead of the homage set. The artwork is Spectrum
HoloByte's: never commit it or publish a build that contains it.

## How faithful is it?

Everything that decides how the game plays was reconstructed from `WELLTRIS.EXE` and is checked
against the original machine code:

- `re/emu/wtemu.py` loads the original executable into the Unicorn CPU emulator, stubs out only
  drawing, image loading and the speaker, replaces the timer, keyboard and far heap, and runs
  the real `game_init` and play loop headless.
- `re/emu/difftest.py` feeds the same key scripts to the original and to `core/` and compares
  the complete game state after every pass of the play loop: walls, floor, stored pieces,
  score, lines, deadlines, the random number generator and the clock. Half of the scripts are
  random keys (with bursts and prefilled floor lines), half are games played by a search bot
  (`tests/botgen.c`) that clears lines and reaches bonus pieces and level ups.
- `re/emu/mutants.py` breaks the core in 15 small ways (timings, scoring, collisions, key
  handling) and checks that the difftest catches every one.

  ```sh
  python3 -m venv ~/tools/venv --system-site-packages && ~/tools/venv/bin/pip install unicorn capstone
  ~/tools/venv/bin/python re/emu/difftest.py 40
  ~/tools/venv/bin/python re/emu/mutants.py 30
  ```

Game tables come from the binary (`re/tools/gen_tables.py`), so no number was typed in by hand.
Findings and addresses are in [`re/NOTES.md`](re/NOTES.md).

Where the original depended on the machine, the port follows the EGA version: the play loop
paces itself on the page flip (60 Hz frames) while gravity, drops and effects run on the
187.17 Hz timer the game programs into the PIT, and the BIOS key repeat is emulated. Sounds are
the original's PC-speaker sweeps, played from the core's log with their exact timing. Pause,
the abort/restart/quit confirmations and the hall of fame follow the code but are not
emulator-tested.

## Tooling

| Tool | Used for | Install |
|------|----------|---------|
| Ghidra (headless) | Decompiling `WELLTRIS.EXE` (16-bit real mode); names in `re/ghidra/names.txt` | zip from GitHub into `~/tools/`, needs `openjdk-21-jdk` |
| Python 3 + capstone, Unicorn | Disassembly, the emulator harness and differential tests | `pip install unicorn capstone` in a venv |
| vtracer, resvg, OpenCV, Pillow | The local artwork tool | see above |
| DOSBox-X + Xvfb | Running the original as a reference, headless screenshots | `apt install dosbox-x xvfb` |
| gcc + SDL2 + CMake | Native build | `apt install libsdl2-dev cmake` |
| Emscripten (emsdk) | WebAssembly build | `git clone emsdk` into `~/tools/emsdk` |

### Demo clip

```sh
./build/wt_botgen 66 2 0 1 0 1000 400 0 66 0 > demo.txt      # the bot's game as a key script
SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy ./build/welltris --size 960x600 --record - --script demo.txt |
  ffmpeg -f rawvideo -pix_fmt bgra -s 960x600 -r 30 -i - -c:v libx264 -crf 27 -pix_fmt yuv420p docs/demo.mp4
```

## Code quality

The core and tests build with `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion
-Wsign-conversion` and more (the frontend without the conversion warnings), and are kept
clean under clang-tidy (`.clang-tidy`), cppcheck and clang-format (`.clang-format`).
CI runs all of this on every push.

## Credits

Welltris © 1989 Doka; American version © 1989 Sphere, Inc. / Spectrum HoloByte. Original
design Alexey Pajitnov and Andrei Snegov; American version by Dan Kaufman, Kevin Seghetti,
Kus Pranawahadi, Greg Marr, Dan Guerra, Jody Sather and Matt Carlstrom. This is an
unofficial fan reimplementation for preservation; no original game files are distributed.
Homage pictures made for this port. Font: Exo 2 (SIL OFL). Text and image decoding:
stb_truetype, stb_image (public domain).

# BlockOut (1989) — decompilation & multiplatform port

BlockOut is a 3D Tetris-like game for DOS (California Dreams / P.Z. Karen Co., 1989).
This repo is a reverse-engineered port of it to portable C + SDL2: it runs natively on
Linux, Windows and macOS, and in a browser via WebAssembly. No original game files are
included or needed to play.

![The original 1989 demo AI playing a 3x3x10 pit until game over](docs/demo-3x3x10.gif)

*The original demo AI, ported from the 1989 code, playing 3-D Mania (3×3×10, basic set)
until the pit fills up. [Full-quality video](docs/demo-3x3x10.mp4).*

The goal has two halves:

1. **Game logic: decompiled faithfully.** Piece sets, the random number generator and
   how it is seeded and used, fall speed and level progression, scoring, layer clears,
   rotation and movement rules, and all timings, expressed in the original timer ticks.
   This is a deterministic, platform-independent C core that is checked frame by frame
   against the original machine code (see [How faithful is it?](#how-faithful-is-it)).
2. **Presentation: modernized.** Rendering, input and audio are written fresh on top of
   the core. The original EGA/CGA/Hercules drawing code is not ported. It is only read
   where it reveals game rules (e.g. what is shown when).

## Layout

| Path        | Contents |
|-------------|----------|
| `core/`     | Game logic reconstructed from `BL2.OVL`: plain C, no I/O, deterministic |
| `src/`      | SDL2 frontend: rendering, input, sound, menus, hall of fame (native and Emscripten) |
| `tests/`    | Replay and bot tools used by the differential tests |
| `web/`      | HTML shell for the browser build |
| `re/`       | Reverse-engineering notes, Ghidra scripts, table generator, emulator harness |
| `docs/`     | Demo clip |

## The original

The reverse-engineering tools in `re/` need your own copy of the DOS release (version
`05-26-89`, the EGA/CGA/Tandy/Hercules build) in `original/`. It is git-ignored and not
distributed. The files the tools were written against:

```
2acc65779b196f17422731339e7a55ff0124898145924c86ca625e6e0a202263  BL2.OVL
174c0644b9d8426165890cab9d5b28ef5835f8393af350a5b38e2a80d65f82ea  BL.EXE
```

- `BL.EXE` is a launcher (Turbo C 2.0). It shows the logo and the graphics-mode menu,
  then loads the game.
- `BL2.OVL` is the game itself. It's a standalone Turbo C MZ executable. This is what
  gets decompiled.
- `*.LBM` are IFF/ILBM images per video mode: `_H` = EGA 640×350, `_L` = 320×200
  (EGA low/CGA/Tandy), `_M` = Hercules 720×348.
- `BLOCKOUT.SET` holds saved settings. `BLSCORE.DAT` / `BLSCORE.IDX` (Hall of Fame)
  are created by the game.

## Downloads

- **Play in the browser:** <https://rembish.github.io/blockout-revamp/>. It works on phones and
  tablets too: touch screens get an on-screen pad (8 directions, like the numpad), the six
  rotation buttons and DROP, and the layout switches to portrait on narrow screens.
- **Windows, macOS, Linux:** pick the latest release, or the artifacts of the newest
  "Binaries" workflow run under Actions. Every build is self-contained (SDL is linked in).
  - Windows: unzip and run `blockout.exe`.
  - macOS: unzip and open `blockout.app`. It is not notarised, so the first time
    right-click → Open (or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine blockout.app`).
  - Linux: `tar xzf blockout-linux-x64.tar.gz && ./blockout/blockout` (x86-64, glibc 2.35+).

## Playing

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| Arrow keys / numpad 8 2 4 6 | move the block |
| Home End PgUp PgDn / numpad 7 1 9 3 | move diagonally |
| Q W E | rotate counter-clockwise (around the three axes) |
| A S D | rotate clockwise |
| Space | drop |
| P | pause, O sound on/off, Esc abort |
| F11 / Alt+Enter | fullscreen |

On a touch screen the same actions are on-screen buttons; tap the pit to resume a pause or
to continue after game over. `--touch` forces the touch layout on desktop.

Menus follow the original (Start Game, Choose Setup, Write Setup, Practice Mode, Demo,
Help), plus a Hall of Fame entry. Leaving a menu alone for a minute starts the demo, as
it did in 1989.

Scores and settings are stored per user (`~/.local/share/BlockOut/BlockOut/` on Linux,
`%APPDATA%\BlockOut\BlockOut\` on Windows, browser storage on the web) in the original
file formats, so `BLSCORE.DAT`, `BLSCORE.IDX` and `BLOCKOUT.SET` from the DOS version can
be copied there (lower-case names).

## Building

Native (Linux, macOS, Windows with any SDL2 package):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j
./build/blockout
```

Browser (Emscripten):

```sh
source ~/tools/emsdk/emsdk_env.sh
emcmake cmake -S . -B build-web
cmake --build build-web -j --target blockout
cd build-web && python3 -m http.server   # open http://localhost:8000/blockout.html
```

The web build is three static files (`blockout.html`, `.js`, `.wasm`) and can be hosted
anywhere. `.github/workflows/pages.yml` builds it on every push to `main` and publishes it
with GitHub Pages (enable it under Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions).

## How faithful is it?

Everything that decides how the game plays was reconstructed from `BL2.OVL` and is
checked against the original machine code:

- `re/emu/` loads the original executable into the Unicorn CPU emulator, stubs out only
  drawing and sound, fakes the BIOS keyboard and timer, and runs the real play loop and
  demo loop headless.
- `re/emu/difftest.py` feeds the same random key scripts (random mashing, a search bot
  that clears layers, pre-filled pits, the demo) to the original and to `core/`, and
  compares the complete game state on every frame.

  ```sh
  python3 -m venv ~/tools/venv --system-site-packages && ~/tools/venv/bin/pip install unicorn
  ~/tools/venv/bin/python re/emu/difftest.py 60
  ```

That covers piece selection and the Turbo C RNG (including the original's reroll quirk),
movement and wall kicks, the rotation queue, gravity per level, the spawn grace, hard
drop and lock delay, layer clears, scoring, level-ups, practice mode and the demo AI.
Pause, sound toggle, Esc and the hall of fame follow the code but aren't emulator-tested.

Game tables are generated from the binary (`re/tools/gen_tables.py`), so no number was
typed in by hand. Findings and addresses are in [`re/NOTES.md`](re/NOTES.md).

Where the original depended on the machine, the port picks the typical behaviour of a
period PC: 60 Hz logic frames (the original waited for EGA retrace each frame) with the
"fast CPU" animation tables, BIOS key repeat (500 ms, 10.9/s), and sound timings
calibrated so the hall-of-fame tune is in tune. Frame pacing can be lowered to
30/20/15 Hz in Change Setup to mimic slower machines.

## Tooling

| Tool | Used for | Install |
|------|----------|---------|
| DOSBox-X | Running the original as a reference; its debugger is used to inspect game state | `apt install dosbox-x` |
| Ghidra (headless) | Disassembly/decompilation of `BL2.OVL` (x86 16-bit real mode) | zip from GitHub into `~/tools/`, needs `openjdk-21-jdk` |
| Python 3 + capstone, Pillow | Ad-hoc disassembly, ILBM decoding, scripted screenshots | `apt install python3-capstone python3-pil` |
| Xvfb | Headless DOSBox-X runs for automated screenshots | `xvfb-run` |
| gcc + SDL2 + CMake | Native build of the port | `apt install libsdl2-dev cmake` |
| Emscripten (emsdk) | WebAssembly build of the port | `git clone emsdk` into `~/tools/emsdk` |
| Unicorn (pip) | Running original code for differential tests | `pip install unicorn` in a venv |

Ghidra has no prebuilt decompiler for Linux on ARM64. Build it from the bundled sources:
`make -C Ghidra/Features/Decompiler/src/decompile/cpp ghidra_opt sleigh_opt ARCH_TYPE=`
(after `mkdir com_opt ghi_opt sla_opt` there) and copy the two binaries to
`Ghidra/Features/Decompiler/os/linux_arm_64/` as `decompile` and `sleigh`.

## Code quality

The core and tests build with `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion
-Wsign-conversion` and more (the frontend without the conversion warnings), and are kept
clean under clang-tidy (`.clang-tidy`), cppcheck and clang-format (`.clang-format`).

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DBO_WERROR=ON && cmake --build build -j
clang-format --dry-run --Werror core/*.h core/bo_core.c src/*.[ch] tests/*.c
clang-tidy -p build core/*.c src/*.c tests/*.c
cppcheck --enable=warning,style,performance,portability --std=c99 -U__EMSCRIPTEN__ \
         --suppress=missingIncludeSystem -I core -I src core src tests
```

CI runs all of this on every push.

## Credits

BlockOut © 1989 P.Z. Karen Co. Development Group / California Dreams. This is an
unofficial fan reimplementation for preservation; no original game files are
distributed. Font: Exo 2 (SIL OFL). Text rendering: stb_truetype (public domain).

# Oh My Lemmings (Rusty Lemmings)

**한국어** | [English](README.en.md)

[![CI](https://github.com/edwardkim/ohmylemmings/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/edwardkim/ohmylemmings/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Play on GitHub Pages](https://github.com/edwardkim/ohmylemmings/actions/workflows/pages.yml/badge.svg)](https://edwardkim.github.io/ohmylemmings/)

고전 DOS 게임 Lemmings의 데이터와 동작을 Rust로 재구현하는 비상업적 토이프로젝트입니다. 결정론적 게임 코어를 렌더링·입출력과 분리하고, SDL2 기반 Native와 WebAssembly 기반 Web에서 공유합니다.

## 공개 목적과 개발 방식

이 프로젝트는 Reverse Engineer Anything(REA)을 사용하지 않고, AI 코딩 에이전트와 함께 고전 게임의 재구현 과정을 탐구하기 위해 공개했습니다. 구현·테스트·플레이 검증·사용자 피드백을 반복하는 개발 과정을 공유하는 것이 목적입니다. REA 미사용은 메인테이너가 밝힌 개발 방식이며, 특정 도구를 사용하지 않았다는 사실이 법적 권한이나 독립 창작을 입증하는 것은 아닙니다.

공개된 **Lemmix** 구현을 물리 규칙·틱·상태 전이의 참고 자료로, **Lemmings.ts**를 데이터 파싱·웹 구조의 참고 자료로 사용했습니다. 원본 게임의 데이터·동작과 비교했으며, OPL 합성기는 기존 오픈소스 구현을 활용·수정했습니다. 참고 소스의 버전과 출처는 [레퍼런스 지도](mydocs/tech_insights/issue-3_reference_code_map.md)와 [고정 소스 목록](assets/manifests/reference_sources.json)에 기록합니다.

따라서 **“역공학 없이 구현했다”, “원본이나 타 구현을 전혀 참고하지 않았다”, “완전한 클린룸 구현이다”라는 주장을 하지 않습니다.** 원본 관찰·데이터 해석과 공개 참조 구현을 활용한 재구현입니다.

## 라이선스와 원본 자산의 경계

- 자체 작성 기여에는 [MIT](LICENSE)가 적용됩니다. 외부 코드에는 각각의 라이선스가 적용되며 [제3자 고지 전문](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt)과 [적용 범위](third_party/README.md)를 확인하세요.
- OPL 합성기는 **LGPL-2.1-or-later**, Native MP3 디코더 Symphonia는 **MPL-2.0**, Noto Sans 글꼴은 **OFL**을 유지합니다. 소스 제공·수정·재링크 안내는 [OPL 문서](crates/lemmings-opl/README.md)와 배포본의 `REBUILD.md`를 따릅니다.
- **원본 DOS 그래픽·레벨·음악·효과음·캐릭터·상표에는 프로젝트 MIT 허가가 적용되지 않습니다.** HD로 다시 그리거나 AI로 생성했다는 사실만으로 원작 관련 권리가 해소되는 것은 아닙니다.
- **현재 v0.3.5 다운로드와 Pages에는 원본 게임 데이터가 포함되어 있습니다.** 확인한 프로젝트 자료에는 그 원본 자산의 공개 재배포 허락 근거가 없습니다. 출처·해시와 라이선스 고지 검사는 배포 권한의 확인을 의미하지 않습니다.

이 안내는 개발 취지와 현재 확인 범위를 설명합니다. 배포 권한 확보나 원본 자산 제거가 완료됐다는 공지가 아닙니다.

## 플레이와 현재 상태

2026-10-25 기준 최신 정식 버전은 **v0.3.5**입니다. 위의 원본 자산 관련 경계를 함께 확인하세요.

- [웹에서 플레이](https://edwardkim.github.io/ohmylemmings/) · [Windows/macOS/Linux/Web 다운로드](https://github.com/edwardkim/ohmylemmings/releases/tag/v0.3.5)
- [v0.3.5 실행 안내](mydocs/releases/issue-252_v0.3.5.md) · [배포·공개 검증](mydocs/reports/issue-252_release_v035.md)
- 강철·건설 계단의 질감과 입체감, HD 지물·특수 배경의 확대 품질, 결정 테마 방향 표지를 개선했습니다.
- WebGPU 지원 브라우저에서는 원본/HD 화면을 GPU로 그리며, 미지원·장치 오류에는 Canvas2D로 전환합니다. Native는 GPU 자동 선택과40FPS 표시 목표를 적용합니다.
- 원본 120레벨, 8가지 기술, HD/원본 화면 전환, 지형 질감·수직벽 개선을 제공합니다.
- 굴착 충격·분진·효과음, 원형 대상 표시, 추락사 충격 표현과 수량0 기술 선택 차단을 제공합니다.
- Web은 현재 플레이에 필요한 HD 자산을 먼저 받고 다음 레벨 자산을 백그라운드로 받습니다. 진행률·재시도·캐시 재사용을 지원합니다.
- F3으로 FPS를 표시하고 F2로 피드백 요약을 복사합니다. [#113 성능 추적](https://github.com/edwardkim/ohmylemmings/issues/113)은 Native 40 FPS 목표 수용 후 메인테이너 지시로 종료했습니다. [종료 기록](mydocs/reports/issue-113_closure.md)에 과거 측정과 현재 범위를 정리했습니다.

Windows는 **Windows 11 x64**를 지원하며 Windows 10은 지원하지 않습니다. macOS는 **13+ Apple Silicon/Intel universal2**이며 ad-hoc 서명·미공증 상태입니다. Linux는 SDL2 runtime이 필요합니다. 압축 파일은 전체를 풀어서 사용하세요.

Web에서는 **MP3 선택**, Native에서는 **F4/Ctrl+O**(macOS **Cmd+O**도 지원), 파일 드롭 또는 `--bgm FILE`로 로컬 음악을 선택합니다. 음악·효과음 음량을 따로 조절할 수 있습니다. Web의 소리는 화면의 **소리 켜기**로 활성화합니다.

## 개발 및 실행

[rust-toolchain.toml](rust-toolchain.toml)이 Rust **1.93.1**과 rustfmt·Clippy를 고정합니다. GNU Make, Python 3.12, SDL2 개발 라이브러리와 WASM 타깃이 필요하며 웹 검사는 Chrome/Chromium을 사용합니다. 플랫폼별 준비는 [Native 안내](apps/desktop/README.md)와 [Web 안내](apps/web/README.md)를 참고하세요.

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo fetch --locked
python3 tools/web_build.py fetch
make check
```

`make check-rust`, `make check-python`, `make check-wasm`, `make check-desktop`, `make check-web`으로 나누어 실행할 수 있습니다. [CI 안내](mydocs/plans/issue-7_continuous_integration.md)와 [Makefile](Makefile)에 세부 명령이 있습니다.

원본을 이용할 권한이 있는 경우의 데이터 준비·식별 절차는 [자산 안내](assets/README.md)에 있습니다. 도구가 파일을 취득할 수 있다는 사실은 이용·재배포 허가가 아닙니다. 로컬에 준비한 데이터로 실행하려면 다음을 사용합니다.

```sh
cargo run --release --locked --offline -p lemmings-desktop -- --assets assets/local/dos-original
```

F/C/E/K/U/M/B/D는 Floater/Climber/Bomber/Blocker/Builder/Miner/Basher/Digger입니다. 기술을 고르고 레밍을 클릭합니다. Space는 일시정지, 위/아래는 생성 속도, 좌/우는 카메라, Esc는 종료입니다. 상세 키와 오디오·HD 옵션은 플랫폼별 안내를 따릅니다.

# Yogho Yogho — rewritten engine

**Play in the browser: https://prodigity.github.io/yogho-yogho/**

The DOS game *Yogho Yogho* (1995, Euphoria) running on an engine rewritten from scratch in C,
for desktop (SDL2) and the web (WebAssembly). Unofficial fan preservation project, not
affiliated with the original makers or brand owners.

## How it was made

- The original program (`YOGHO.EXE`, 16-bit real-mode Borland C++ with hand-written assembly) and
  its data file were reverse-engineered statically (Ghidra + capstone), including the 12 level
  overlays (code that ships inside `YOGHODAT.DAT`), the AdLib S3M music driver and the end-credits
  program.
- Every routine was ported to C, keeping the original's data layout (a 1 MB real-mode memory model
  with the exe image and DGROUP at the original segments), its timer-interrupt frame scheduler and
  a model of the VGA hardware (Mode X planes, CRTC/attribute/DAC registers), so the original's
  quirks are kept.
- Faithfulness is checked against the original running under the DOSBox-X debugger: snapshots of
  the original's memory are replayed through the port with the same input, and the game state is
  compared byte for byte (`--snapplay`), plus the music driver state (`--opltrace`).

The engine reads the original game files at runtime: `YOGHO.EXE` (data tables only — it is never
executed) and `YOGHODAT.DAT`. They are not part of the source tree.

## Build

Desktop (Windows, MSVC Build Tools 2022 + SDL2 VC dev package): `build.bat` → `build\yogho.exe`;
run it next to `YOGHO.EXE`, `YOGHODAT.DAT`, `YOGHOHI.DAT` (or pass `--exe`, `--data`).
Web (emsdk 3.1.64): `build-web.bat <folder with the game files>` → `build-web\`.

Developer tools: `--script file [--fast]` (scripted input, dumps), `--snapplay` / `--snaprun`
(replay a DOSBox snapshot), `--opltrace` (AdLib register stream).

Conventions for the code: `PORTING.md`. Third-party: Nuked-OPL3 (LGPL-2.1, `third_party/`),
SDL2 (zlib).

# Galaga '94 — native port

A native Windows and Linux port of **Galaga '94 v2.1** (1994), the DOS shoot-'em-up by Arnold Pichler / APSS Austria. The game was released as *MailWare*: free to play and share, with a request to write to the author.

The port runs the original game code, not a remake. `GALAGA.EXE` (Turbo Pascal 6, 16-bit real mode) is **statically recompiled to C**: every x86 instruction becomes a line of C. That C runs on a small machine layer, and SDL2 stands in for the 1994 PC hardware:

| 1994 hardware | Port |
|---|---|
| VGA mode 13h / Mode X (planar, page flipping, 70 Hz retrace) | `src/vga.c` → SDL texture, 4:3, resizable, Alt+Enter for fullscreen |
| Keyboard interrupt (INT 9, port 60h scancodes) | SDL keys → XT scancodes; a game controller works alongside the keys |
| BIOS timer tick (INT 8 → INT 1Ch, 18.2 Hz) | real-time PIT |
| Sound Blaster through `FX_SB.DRV` (CT-VOICE) | `.VOC` decoding through SDL audio |
| PC speaker | square wave |
| DOS files | the `data/` folder; high scores go to the user's save folder |

Gameplay, speed and timing are the original's. The game paces itself on the 70 Hz VGA retrace, so it plays like it did on a fast 1994 PC.

## Playing

Run `galaga94` (`galaga94.exe` on Windows) next to the `data/` folder. `-f` starts fullscreen.

| | Keyboard | Controller |
|---|---|---|
| Move | ← → | D-pad / left stick |
| Fire | Right Shift (also Space or Left Ctrl) | A / right trigger |
| Megabomb | Enter | B |
| Start / continue | ↑ | D-pad up |
| New game (title) | F1 | Start |
| Difficulty (title) | F2 | Y |
| Back to title | Esc | Back |
| Quit (title) | F10 | |

High scores are saved to `%APPDATA%\APSS\Galaga94\` on Windows and `~/.local/share/APSS/Galaga94/` on Linux.

## Building

`src/game.c` is generated, and it's checked in so a build only needs a C compiler and SDL2.

- **Windows:** MSYS2 `mingw32` gcc plus the SDL2 VC dev package. Run `./build.sh` (set `SDL=` to the SDL2 folder; `CONSOLE=1` gives a console build).
- **Linux:** `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`, then `./build.sh`.

To regenerate `src/game.c` from `data/GALAGA.EXE` (needs Python and `capstone`), run `REGEN=1 ./build.sh`.

Debug options:
- `CFLAGS=-DTRACE` logs every routine the first time it runs, plus frame rate, keys and sounds.
- `GALAGA_INPUT="ms:scancode,..."` and `GALAGA_SHOT="ms:file.bmp,..."` script keypresses and screenshots.
- `GALAGA_QUIT_MS` exits after a set time.

## Layout

- `tools/recomp.py`: the recompiler. It descends from the entry point, every procedure prologue and the hand-written asm routines, then sweeps the gaps.
- `tools/disasm.py`: listing for reading the code (`out/galaga.asm`).
- `src/cpu.h`: registers, memory and 286 flag semantics.
- `src/runtime.c`: loader, run loop, interrupts, DOS/BIOS.
- `src/vga.c`, `src/sound.c`, `src/platform.c`: the devices and the SDL front end.
- `data/`: the game files, unchanged from `reference-files/gal94_v2.zip` except `GALAGA.CFG`, which is set to Sound Blaster sound. `SETUP.EXE` isn't needed.

## Credits

Galaga '94 © 1994 Arnold Pichler, APSS Austria, distributed as MailWare. "Galaga" is a Namco trademark; this is the 1994 fan game, not Namco's.

# Jewel Thief — a faithful native port A native reimplementation of **Jewel Thief** (Paul Ligeski / ServantWare, 1991–1993), the 16-bit Windows 3.x game where the mouse cursor is a thief stealing jewels from guards. Rebuilt in C99 from a reverse engineering of the original, it plays like the original, down to its formulas, its pace and its quirks, built for every Windows from XP to 11, for Linux, for the browser, for Android and for MS-DOS on any 386. The repository holds **no original code or assets**. The game loads its graphics, cursors, menu, dialogs and texts at runtime from your own copy of the original `JWLTHIEF.EXE` v1.4. ## Highlights - **Same rules, same numbers.** Guard counts and speeds, jewel placement, scoring, extra lives and the order of every `rand()` call are transcribed from the original code, including the Microsoft C random number generator. - **Same pace.** The game ticks every 54.9 ms, the Windows 3.1 timer rate the original actually ran at, also while dialogs are open. - **Same look.** The seven scenes are redrawn from the original's shapes and coordinates, and sprites get the colors they had in 256 colors on any display, without the original's high-color glitch. - **Same dialogs and menu on Windows.** They are built from the original's own Windows 3.x templates, converted to Win32 on the fly. The MS-DOS build draws them itself from the same templates, on a Windows 3.1 desktop of its own. The Linux build uses native GTK 4 menus and dialogs instead, the browser build HTML ones and the Android build Android ones, still with the original's texts; only their gameplay is kept faithful. - **One game everywhere.** The browser, Android and MS-DOS builds run the same C code, compiled to WebAssembly, for the NDK and with DJGPP, so they play exactly like the desktop ones. That code uses no floating point, so it runs on a 386 without a math coprocessor. - **Compatible settings.** Options and high scores live in the original's `SERVANT.INI`, in its own format, next to `JWLTHIEF.EXE`. The browser keeps the same keys and values in its local storage. How the original works and what the port does about it is documented in [`docs/research.md`](docs/research.md). ## Playing 1. Get the original **Jewel Thief v1.4**; it ships in `JWLTHF14.ZIP`. The executable is recognized by its SHA-256, whatever its name. See [`original/`](original/README.md). 2. Put `jthief_32.exe` or `jthief_64.exe` in the folder that holds `JWLTHIEF.EXE`, and run it. The folder can also be given on the command line: ```sh jthief_64.exe [--debug] [folder of JWLTHIEF.EXE] ``` | Executable | Built for | |-----------------|-------------------------------| | `jthief_32.exe` | Windows XP to Windows 11 | | `jthief_64.exe` | 64-bit Windows | | `jthief` | Linux, with GTK 4 | | `app-debug.apk` | Android 8.0 and newer | | `JTHIEF.EXE` | MS-DOS, on a 386 or newer | ### In the browser Open the page and pick or drop your `JWLTHIEF.EXE`. It is checked and read in the browser, never uploaded, and kept in the browser's storage so it is asked for only once. The game is shown at the largest whole number of screen pixels per game pixel, up to two, so it stays sharp at any zoom. ### On Android The first start asks for your `JWLTHIEF.EXE` and copies it into the app, where `SERVANT.INI` is kept too. The screen works as a trackpad: drag anywhere and the thief moves as far as your finger, so it never jumps and stays put when you lift your finger, like a mouse let go. Back pauses, and the pause box holds the menu. ### On MS-DOS `JTHIEF.EXE` needs a 386 or newer, with or without a math coprocessor, 4 MB of RAM, a VGA card and a mouse driver, such as [CuteMouse](https://cutemouse.sourceforge.net/) (`CTMOUSE`) or `MOUSE.COM`. It runs on MS-DOS 3.3 and newer, including the MS-DOS mode of Windows 95 and 98, and in [DOSBox](https://www.dosbox-staging.org/). Put it next to `JWLTHIEF.EXE`, or pass the folder that holds the original: ```bat C:\GAMES\JTHIEF> JTHIEF C:\> JTHIEF C:\GAMES\JTHIEF ``` The DPMI host, CWSDPMI, is built into the executable. Like every DJGPP program, it may leave an empty `CWSDPMI.SWP` in the root of drive C:, its swap file. The screen is drawn as Windows 3.1 showed the game on a VGA: the 500x300 window on a 640x480 desktop, with its menu bar and dialogs. Alt or F10 opens the menu, as in Windows, and Alt-F4 quits. ### Controls | Input | Action | |-------|--------| | Mouse | Move the thief; touch a jewel to take it | | F2 | New game | | F3 | Pause | ### Debug mode `--debug`, on MS-DOS too, or `?debug` in the browser's address, turns on keys the original never had, and the title bar shows `[DEBUG]` while it is on. On Android, the app's `debug` extra adds the same commands to the pause box: ```sh adb shell am start -n io.github.hfantini.jthief/.MainActivity --ez debug true ``` | Key | Action | |-------------------------|--------| | Home | Toggle god mode: guards and leaving the field cost no lives | | Page Up / Page Down | Next / previous level | ## Building The Windows executables are cross-compiled with MinGW-w64, and the Linux one needs GTK 4; all need CMake 3.21 or newer. On Fedora: ```sh sudo dnf install cmake mingw32-gcc mingw64-gcc # wine, to run the builds on Linux sudo dnf install gcc gtk4-devel # the Linux build sudo dnf install nodejs # the browser build, with emsdk below ``` The browser build compiles the game with [Emscripten](https://emscripten.org/), installed with its SDK, which the `wasm` preset finds through `$EMSDK`: ```sh git clone https://github.com/emscripten-core/emsdk.git ~/emsdk ~/emsdk/emsdk install latest && ~/emsdk/emsdk activate latest source ~/emsdk/emsdk_env.sh # in each shell, or in ~/.bashrc ``` The MS-DOS build uses [DJGPP](https://www.delorie.com/djgpp/), the GCC for DOS, from the prebuilt toolchain of [build-djgpp](https://github.com/andrewwutw/build-djgpp), with the CWSDPMI DPMI host beside it. The `dos` preset finds it through `$DJGPP_PREFIX`, or in `~/djgpp`. Its `ar` needs the flex runtime, which Fedora ships apart: ```sh sudo dnf install libfl2 dosbox-staging # dosbox-staging, to run the build curl -L https://github.com/andrewwutw/build-djgpp/releases/download/v3.4/djgpp-linux64-gcc1220.tar.bz2 \ | tar -xj -C ~ curl -L https://www.delorie.com/pub/djgpp/current/v2misc/csdpmi7b.zip -o /tmp/csdpmi7b.zip unzip /tmp/csdpmi7b.zip -d ~/djgpp/cwsdpmi ``` Each preset builds in `build//` and puts the game in `bin//`: | Preset | Output | |-----------------|------------------------------| | `win32-release` | `bin/release/jthief_32.exe` | | `win64-release` | `bin/release/jthief_64.exe` | | `win32-debug` | `bin/debug/jthief_32.exe` | | `win64-debug` | `bin/debug/jthief_64.exe` | | `linux` | `bin/debug/jthief` and tests | | `wasm` | `build/wasm/jthief.js` and `jthief.wasm`, for the browser build | | `dos` | `bin/release/JTHIEF.EXE` | ```sh cmake --preset win64-release cmake --build --preset win64-release wine bin/release/jthief_64.exe original/ cmake --preset linux cmake --build --preset linux bin/debug/jthief original/ cmake --preset dos cmake --build --preset dos cp original/JWLTHIEF.EXE bin/release/ dosbox bin/release/JTHIEF.EXE ``` DOSBox always emulates a math coprocessor and fast hardware. To try the slowest machine the DOS build supports, a 386 with no coprocessor and a plain VGA, or one close to a Pentium II, [DOSBox-X](https://dosbox-x.com/) takes the settings in `tools/dosbox/`: ```sh flatpak install flathub com.dosbox_x.DOSBox-X flatpak run com.dosbox_x.DOSBox-X -conf tools/dosbox/386.conf bin/release/JTHIEF.EXE ``` The browser build is driven by npm from the repository's root: `npm run wasm` runs the `wasm` preset, `npm run dev` serves the game at `http://localhost:5173` and reloads it on changes, and `npm run build` puts a static site in `bin/web/`: ```sh npm install npm run wasm npm run dev ``` The Android build needs JDK 17 or newer and the Android SDK with the command-line tools, platform 36, NDK 30 and CMake 4.1.2, with `ANDROID_HOME` pointing at the SDK. Its Gradle project in `src/platform/android/` builds the game with the repository's `CMakeLists.txt` and writes everything to `build/android/`; the Gradle wrapper downloads Gradle itself: ```sh cd src/platform/android ./gradlew assembleDebug # build/android/app/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk ./gradlew installDebug # onto the phone adb is connected to ``` Android launchers only show icons built into the app. When `original/` holds the original, the build makes the launcher icon from the original's own icon, with a small tool it compiles from the game's C code with the host's `cc`; the icon stays in `build/`, and such an app is for your own device. Without the original, the app gets the port's own icon. The tests run on the `linux` preset; those needing the original look for it in `original/` (override with `-DJT_ORIGINAL_DIR=`) and are skipped without it: ```sh cmake --preset linux && cmake --build --preset linux ctest --test-dir build/linux --output-on-failure ``` ## Architecture Everything but `src/platform/` is portable C99 with no Windows, GTK, browser, Android or DOS dependency, and integer arithmetic only. The browser build compiles it to WebAssembly together with `platform/web/bridge`, a flat API that the TypeScript side in `platform/web/app` calls: the browser owns the loop, and the C code answers ticks and mouse moves and renders the frames. The Android build works the same way, with `platform/android/jni` as the C side of its Kotlin app. The MS-DOS build has no system to lean on: `platform/dos` drives the VGA, the mouse, the keyboard and the BIOS clock itself, and redraws the Windows 3.1 screen around the game, menus and dialogs included. ```mermaid flowchart TD platform["platform/win32, gtk, web, android, dos
window, input, clock, dialogs"] profile["profile
SERVANT.INI"] render["render
frames and scenery"] core["core
rules, RNG, high scores, settings"] gfx["gfx
framebuffer, DIBs, shapes"] assets["assets
bitmaps, cursors, dialogs, texts"] neres["neres
NE resource reader"] original["original
finds JWLTHIEF.EXE by hash"] platform --> render platform --> profile profile --> core platform --> gfx platform --> core platform --> assets render --> core render --> gfx render --> assets assets --> gfx assets --> neres assets --> original ``` | Path | Purpose | |--------------------------|---------| | `src/core/` | Game rules and state, the Microsoft C `rand()`, high scores, settings | | `src/render/` | Draws frames and the seven scenes into a framebuffer | | `src/gfx/` | 32-bit framebuffer, DIB and cursor decoding, the original's sprite raster operation, GDI-like shapes | | `src/assets/` | Reads bitmaps, cursors, icons, resources and texts from the original executable | | `src/neres/` | Reader for 16-bit NE executables: resources and data segment | | `src/original/` | Finds the user's v1.4 executable by its SHA-256 | | `src/profile/` | Options and high scores in `SERVANT.INI` | | `src/common/` | SHA-256, file system and INI helpers | | `src/platform/win32/` | Window, menu, clock thread, dialogs, Windows 3.x template conversion | | `src/platform/gtk/` | Linux: GTK 4 window, menu, clock thread and dialogs | | `src/platform/web/bridge/` | Browser: the C API compiled to WebAssembly with the game | | `src/platform/web/app/` | Browser: TypeScript page, canvas, clock, menu and dialogs | | `src/platform/android/` | Android: Gradle project, Kotlin app (view, trackpad, clock, dialogs) and `jni/`, its C side | | `src/platform/dos/` | MS-DOS: VGA, mouse, keyboard and clock, and a Windows 3.1 desktop with the original's menu and dialogs | | `tests/` | CTest suite | | `tools/ne.py` | Inspect an NE executable or extract its resources | | `tools/ghidra/` | Headless Ghidra pipeline used to reverse engineer the original | | `tools/dosbox/` | DOSBox-X settings for a 386 without coprocessor and for a Pentium II | | `cmake/` | MinGW-w64 toolchains for 32- and 64-bit Windows, DJGPP toolchain for MS-DOS | | `docs/research.md` | The original, its internals, and the port's decisions | ## Reverse engineering The port was written from a static analysis of the original in [Ghidra](https://ghidra-sre.org/) 12, driven from the command line: ```sh tools/ghidra/analyze.sh # import, Win16 fixups, auto-analysis, recovered symbols tools/ghidra/export.sh # decompiled C and TSV indexes of functions, globals, strings ``` `analyze.sh` keeps its Ghidra project in `../.ghidra` and `export.sh` writes to `../.re/export`, both outside the repository: they derive from the copyrighted original and are never committed. The scripts fix what Ghidra gets wrong in Microsoft C Win16 code (inline switch tables, FAR PASCAL callbacks, Win16 API prototypes) and apply the names and types recovered so far, kept in [`tools/ghidra/symbols/jwlthief.symbols`](tools/ghidra/symbols/jwlthief.symbols). ## Credits Jewel Thief was written by Paul Ligeski and published by ServantWare. This project is an independent reimplementation for preservation and study; it contains none of the original's code or assets, and needs a copy of the original to run.

# narrator-ts

TypeScript reimplementation of the Amiga's speech pair: `translator.library`
(English to phonemes) and `narrator.device` 33.2 (phoneme formant synthesis).

Output is Paula-native — 8-bit signed samples and the period they were written
with. Verified against the real binaries running under a 68000 emulator:
byte-exact translation on 15,405 phrases, sample-exact synthesis end to end.

```sh
npm install narrator-ts
```

```ts
import { speak } from 'narrator-ts'
import { translate } from 'narrator-ts/translator'
import rules from 'narrator-ts/reference/nrl-table.json' with { type: 'json' }
import voice from 'narrator-ts/reference/voice-free.json' with { type: 'json' }

const { phonemes } = translate('hello world', rules)   // '/HEHLOW WERLD '
const { pcm, sampleRate } = speak(Buffer.from(phonemes, 'latin1'), voice)
// Int8Array(26112) at 22030 Hz
```

Both tables are the free ones, so that runs with nothing else installed. Swap
either for an extracted Amiga table to get the authentic voice — see below.

`pcm` is 8-bit signed. `speak` takes `narrator_rb`'s own parameters —
`pitch`, `rate`, `sex`, `mode`, `sampfreq`, `mouths` — and returns one entry
per sentence alongside the joined samples, because that is how the device
produces them.

## Voices

A voice is ~12 KB of tables: formant frequencies and amplitudes per phoneme,
durations, allophonic rewrite rules, the glottal waveform, fricative noise.
They are a *parameter*, not built in.

**The authentic Amiga voice** is Commodore and SoftVoice's, so it is not in
this repository. Extract it from Workbench disk images you already own:

```sh
python3 tools/extract-devices.py /path/to/workbench-disks -o fixtures/amiga
python3 tools/gen-voice.py   fixtures/amiga/narrator_device-33.2-*.bin     -o data
python3 tools/gen-tables.py  fixtures/amiga/translator_library-33.2-1*.bin -o data
```

**The free voice** is `reference/voice-free.json`, built from published
phonetics by `tools/gen-free-voice.py` and owing nothing to anyone. It is the
default, so a fresh clone speaks. It is not the Amiga's voice and does not
claim to be — `reference/README.md` says what is measured and what is still
provisional.

The letter-to-sound half has its free equivalent too, and is the default when
no Amiga table has been extracted:

```ts
import nrl from 'narrator-ts/reference/nrl-table.json' with { type: 'json' }
translate('hello world', nrl)   // '/HEHLOW WERLD '
```

That is the rule set of NRL Report 7948 (Elovitz et al., 1976 — a US
Government work), rebuilt from the report alone. It is not byte-compatible
with the Amiga and is not meant to be: 64.6% of distinct words match.
`research/03-nrl-provenance.md` has the measurements.

## Command line

```sh
npm run say -- 'hello world' -o hello.wav          # the free voice
npm run say -- 'hello world' -o hello.wav -V 33.2  # an extracted Amiga one
npm run say -- -p '/HEH4LOW WER4LD' -o hello.wav
npm run say -- 'is this a question' --pitch 200 --rate 100
```

`--pitch --rate --sex --mode --sampfreq --mouths` are `narrator_rb`'s own
fields. `npm run say` with no arguments prints them.

Every tool under `tools/` takes `--help`.

## AROS resource export

Create the versioned IFF resource consumed by AROS `translator.library`,
`narrator.device`, and `speech.device`:

```sh
npm run export:aros -- -o speech.iff
npm run export:aros -- -o speech.iff \
  --translator data/translator-33.2.json \
  --voice data/narrator-33.2.json \
  --translator-license "User supplied; redistribution not granted" \
  --voice-license "User supplied; redistribution not granted"
npm run export:aros -- -o speech-resource.c --format c
```

The first command uses the redistributable reference tables. The second uses
locally extracted authentic tables; the resulting file has the same legal
status as those inputs and should not be redistributed.
The C form contains the identical IFF payload as a byte array for ROM builds.

`FORM NARR` uses ordinary length-delimited Latin-1 IFF chunks rather than an
embedded serialization format. `VERS` is the binary resource schema version;
`FVER` records the narrator-ts package version. `TVER`/`TSRC`/`TLIC` describe
the translator and `VVER`/`VSRC`/`VLIC` describe the voice, followed by their
`LTRS` and `NVOI` table chunks. The built-in free inputs are labelled public
domain. Explicit table paths conservatively default to `User supplied;
redistribution not granted`; the two `--*-license` options override that text.

## Status

| | |
|---|---|
| translator | byte-exact against all 6 shipped builds |
| narrator 33.2 | byte-exact front half, sample-exact renderer, end to end |
| free letter-to-sound table | built, divergence measured |
| free voice | **speaks**; texture within a few percent of 33.2's, no allophonic rules yet |

`narrator.device` 37.7 is a rewrite and is **out of scope** — one voice done
properly. 1.6, 31.13, 33.2 and 36.9 are sample-identical over 4,865 phrases,
so 33.2 covers four of the five shipped builds anyway.

## Licence

Code is MIT.

The Amiga binaries and everything derived by running them are not
redistributable and are gitignored: `fixtures/amiga/*.bin`,
`fixtures/golden/`, `data/`. None has ever been committed.

`reference/` is the opposite — material that can be redistributed, with its
provenance recorded in `reference/README.md`.

`narrator.device`'s copyright line reads *Mark Barton / Joseph Katz*. It was
licensed in from SoftVoice, Inc.; Commodore never owned it.

## Documentation

| | |
|---|---|
| `docs/development.md` | building the oracle, regenerating fixtures, coverage |
| `research/00-findings.md` | what the binaries turned out to be |
| `research/01-translator.md` | the letter-to-sound engine |
| `research/02-narrator.md` | the synthesizer, stage by stage |
| `research/03-nrl-provenance.md` | which rules came from NRL and which SoftVoice added |
